title: Sources & Open Questions
text:
Resolved

UCLA’s ICPSR founding-member status
Confirmed against the actual 1962 document, not just a later recollection or a university’s own marketing page. Warren Miller’s own August 1962 founding memo lists “University of California at Los Angeles” among the institutions participating “as of July 30, 1962.” See miller-1962-considerations.md. This does not resolve the exact headcount (see below) or Marvick’s personal role (see below).

title: Sources & Open Questions
text:
Open conflicts

The “8 founding members” headcount: not simply wrong, now genuinely unresolved
This looked settled, then got more complicated instead of less. Two independent counts put the full initial ICPSR membership above 8: Erik Austin’s founding-years essay counts 22 institutions from membership records, and Warren Miller’s own August 1962 memo names 21 directly, dated “as of July 30, 1962.” Both include UCLA. Neither has an “8” anywhere.
But ICPSR’s current director, Maggie Levenstein, independently used the figure “8” during a UCLA visit, not obviously drawing on UCLA’s own page. And ICPSR’s own institutional archive at the Bentley Historical Library holds a folder titled “Committee of Eight, Correspondence and Minutes, 1962-1963,” per its finding aid (umich-bhl-9938-finding-aid.md). A plausible reconciliation: “8” refers to a specific founding committee, not the full 21/22-institution membership roster. Both numbers could be correct, describing two different things. Not confirmed. Nobody has read that folder, and nobody has asked Levenstein what she meant. Either would settle this faster than more inference.


Eve Fielder’s SRC directorship: 1964 or 1976?
Three internal sources say the archive merged into the Survey Research Center in 1964 “under Eve Fielder.” A Fielder obituary cited in the deep-research report says she became SRC’s first director in 1976, the same year SRC was reportedly incorporated into ISSR. Not resolved. Needs a documentary check (SRC records, UCLA Sociology/Political Science department histories, or an earlier obituary detail) before either date gets used as fact in the narrative.


1977’s institutional home: four accounts, four answers

Both 2017 decks: the archive came under ISSR.
The Dataverse About page: Donald Treiman designed the framework; no institutional home named.
The book-chapter draft: the archive was created “as part of the Survey Research Center”; no ISSR mention.
External evidence (UCLA’s 1977–78 General Catalog, per the deep-research report): ISSR is the named parent, with SRC as a component under it.

The catalog evidence points toward ISSR being correct and the book chapter’s SRC-only framing being the error. That’s an inference though, not a confirmed correction. Verify against the catalog directly.


Marvick’s claimed ICPSR founding role
Separate question from the headcount above, and also not resolved, though closer than it was. ICPSR’s own first annual report names its initial council members, and Marvick isn’t among them. Neither Austin’s founding-years essay nor Miller’s own 1962 memo mentions him, though Miller’s memo doesn’t name any individual faculty member from any institution, since the Consortium was explicitly built on “institutional rather than individual participation,” so that absence carries less weight than his absence from the council-member list does. What changed: Eulau’s 1999 memorial establishes that Marvick and Miller were close personal friends and research collaborators for a full decade before either the archive or ICPSR existed, together at Michigan’s Survey Research Center in the early 1950s. That’s a real, documented mechanism for “through his efforts” to be true informally, even though no document yet says it directly. His formally documented ICPSR role is governing-board service from 1964, rising to chair of the ICPR Council in 1966-67 (per Eulau), all after founding. The Dataverse page’s “through [Marvick’s] efforts, UCLA was one of the founding members” is now plausible rather than simply unsupported, but still not confirmed by any document found so far.


Donald Treiman’s relationship to ISSR
The Dataverse page credits him with designing the 1977 framework but doesn’t mention ISSR. The deep-research report notes his CV supports depositor and intellectual involvement but not necessarily a formal ISSR title. Whether he was an ISSR-affiliated director or a faculty collaborator outside ISSR’s own leadership structure is unresolved. His living status is also unconfirmed.


Newsletters
No digitized ISSR/SSDA newsletter or annual-report run has been found in any public index checked (UCLA General Catalog, eScholarship, Internet Archive, HathiTrust, Google Books, UCLA Digital Library). This is a negative search result. It means “not found here,” not “doesn’t exist.” The physical-location inquiry (UCLA University Archives, former staff) is the live lead for this, checking the week of 2026-08-03.
Tim recalls the newsletters referred to the unit informally as “the Data Archive,” and that this usage spanned multiple formal institutional eras (ISSR, the ISR rename, standalone SSDA). Not yet confirmed since the newsletters themselves haven’t been found. Worth watching for once they turn up: it would mean the informal “Data Archive” self-identification persisted underneath at least three formal name changes, which would be a nice thread connecting the 2017 internal decks’ own tagline (“providing archive and data services since 1961”) back through the whole ISSR era.

section: How to read confidence notes on this site
text:
How to read confidence notes on this site
Where a claim in the narrative chapters carries a confidence note, it follows this rough scale:

Very high: a primary document in hand (CV, MOU, obituary, catalog entry)
High: a named, dated claim from a credible source, not yet cross-checked
Moderate: plausible, sourced, but only one account exists
Disputed / unresolved: multiple sources actively disagree

title: Joining the Library & the Data Science Center (2014–present)
text:
NoteSource



This chapter draws heavily on a full book-chapter draft already written by DSC staff (evidence/data-sci-libraries_chapter_edits.md, “From a Data Archive to Data Science,” Dennis, Yao, Phan, Allen, Jamison, Daniels, Ali) and the 2014 SSDA→ Library MOU (evidence/ssda-library-mou.md). Most of what follows can be adapted directly from that chapter rather than rewritten from scratch.

title: Joining the Library & the Data Science Center (2014–present)
text:
The 2014 transfer
The Social Science Data Archive transferred from UCLA’s Social Sciences Division to the UCLA Library via a Memorandum of Understanding, drafted and effective November 1, 2014, and executed August 2015 (Virginia Steel, University Librarian, 2015-08-04; Alessandro Duranti, Dean of Social Sciences, 2015-08-10). The MOU transferred:

2.0 FTE and approximately $245,000 in permanent funds
Approximately $29,000 in permanent subscription funds (ICPSR, Roper, UC Berkeley/SDA, Colectica/Algenta)
A “Data Archive Purchase Fund” foundation gift (~$10,477)
Two staff with continuous service: Elizabeth “Libbie” Stephenson (Librarian) and Jina/Jamie Jamison (Programmer/Analyst), a director and a data archivist per the book chapter

The MOU also included a consultation clause: if the Library later made “substantial changes to the operations of Social Sciences Data Archives,” the Library and the Social Sciences Division were to meet and ensure continuity of faculty access to services.
By the 2010s, SSDA’s narrow service profile (survey research data collection, management, and preservation) no longer matched researchers’ emerging needs across formats (text, image, audio) and disciplines. The move to the Library was framed as a way to modernize services rather than simply relocate an existing one.
Per Tim Dennis, Todd Grappone, then UCLA Library’s AUL for Digital Initiatives and Information Technology, shepherded SSDA’s transfer into the Library. This isn’t yet documented in any source beyond Tim’s own account as a direct participant. Grappone later became University Librarian at UC Santa Barbara in 2025; see People for his fuller career record.

title: Joining the Library & the Data Science Center (2014–present)
text:
The 2018 rebrand: Data Science Center
In Spring 2018, the unit was formally restructured and renamed the Data Science Center (DSC), with a new mission statement:

The Data Science Center’s mission is to foster a welcoming research community by developing data literacy and foundational coding skills through consulting and education. We support researchers throughout the full data life cycle of activities: planning research projects and data management plans; data acquisition, storage, cleaning and usage; analysis; publication; curation; and preservation.

The DSC retained SSDA’s core services (data literacy, data management, data discovery) while broadening scope to serve any discipline, not only the social sciences. Per Tim, Todd Grappone also coined the “Data Science Center” name and helped design and reorient the 2018 service model, alongside the 2018 book chapter’s co-authors.

title: Joining the Library & the Data Science Center (2014–present)
text:
The Carpentries
The DSC joined The Carpentries, a volunteer-led data science teaching organization, in 2017 (ahead of the formal 2018 rebrand) to scale instruction with a limited staff. By the time of the book chapter’s writing, Carpentries membership at UCLA had grown to over ten instructors across six departments, including the entire DSC team. Tim Dennis won The Carpentries’ 2018 Community Service Award, cited for teaching over 20 workshops and establishing Library Carpentry as a Lesson Program within the organization.

title: Joining the Library & the Data Science Center (2014–present)
text:
UCLA Dataverse
Before joining the Library, SSDA’s collections lived on Harvard’s hosted Dataverse instance. In 2018, the DSC stood up a local UCLA Dataverse instance, extending the same repository model (DDI metadata support, tiered curation, license restriction) to the whole UCLA research community. Research groups can sponsor their own branded sub-collections within it. Jina “Jamie” Jamison, whose UCLA service traces back through the 2014 transfer, has led on UCLA Dataverse since: she represented UCLA at the Dataverse Community Meeting 2021 and authored the platform’s preservation documentation.

title: Joining the Library & the Data Science Center (2014–present)
text:
Staffing growth
The unit grew from two staff at the 2014 transfer to five full-time staff, adding roles in GIS (Spatial Data Science Librarian), computational/data-science facilitation, and machine learning. Most of that growth came from redesigning existing library positions rather than net-new hiring, supplemented by a Carpentries-trained instructor pool and a student program modeled on Carleton College’s DataSquad. Doug Daniels joined the DSC team in 2020 as Emerging Technologies Librarian, folding the Lux Lab’s 3D printing, scanning, and drone mapping/imaging services into the center’s portfolio; he won UCLA’s 2026 Librarian of the Year Award for that work.

title: Joining the Library & the Data Science Center (2014–present)
text:
A note on scope
This history stops at the DSC’s structure as it stood before 2026. As of publication, the unit’s organizational status is under internal review. This history does not attempt to characterize an unresolved process. It will be revisited once that process concludes.

title: Origins (1961–1977)
text: UCLA’s data archive lineage begins with Dwaine Marvick, a UCLA political science professor who founded the Political Behavior Archive (PBA) in 1961. Rice & Southall (2016), The Data Librarian’s Handbook, Table 1.1, situates it in the field’s founding cohort: “UCLA Data Services, 1961” ranks as the fourth-oldest social-science data library or service in their sample, after Roper Center (1957), Berkeley (1958), and GESIS (1960), and ahead of ICPSR itself (1962).

title: Origins (1961–1977)
section: Why archives like this one emerged
text:
Why archives like this one emerged
UCLA’s archive is one local expression of a broader postwar development in empirical social science. It wasn’t the product of a single, unified “movement” with one agreed rationale. It’s better described as a family of related infrastructure-building projects, and contemporaries were already discussing them comparatively by the mid-1960s: Ralph Bisco’s 1966 review in the American Political Science Review treats Roper, Berkeley, Michigan, and European archives as one emerging domain.
The multi-causal explanation that survives scrutiny: the growth of survey research and behavioral political science produced large bodies of reusable observations. The expense of new surveys created an incentive to preserve and share existing ones. Punch cards, tabulating equipment, and later magnetic tape made large-scale reuse technically possible. Foundations, federal agencies, and membership consortia made the resulting infrastructure sustainable. Training new quantitative researchers wasn’t incidental either. At ICPSR especially, it was a founding purpose, not a service layered on afterward.
One correction to how this was framed internally: centralized campus computing is better documented as an enabling condition and a bottleneck than as the originating cause. The clearest founding documents (ICPSR’s 1962 memorandum, Roper’s founding rationale, the UK Data Archive’s founding committee) foreground research demand, cost, and coordination problems. Computing shows up as the means the solution operated through, not the reason the problem became urgent.
That framing holds up against the actual founding document. Warren Miller’s August 1962 memo to ISR director Rensis Likert, laying out the case for what became ICPSR, opens with the research problem, not a technology problem: “The rapid increase in scholarly interest in the kinds of data which survey research can provide has far outstripped the availability of the survey mechanism to the interested scholar. This hiatus has become a matter of serious concern to many social scientists.” Computing gets no mention in his stated rationale at all.

title: Origins (1961–1977)
text:
A founding member of ICPSR, 1962
UCLA was among the founding member institutions of the Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research (ICPSR), established in 1962 by political scientist Warren E. Miller to solve an organizational bottleneck in the production of empirical political science. Heavily demanded election-study data needed permanent preservation and dissemination, but so did training new researchers to use it and coordinating a scattered research community. Its founding memorandum set four objectives, conceived together rather than as separable services: developing data resources, formal quantitative training, stimulating new research, and a clearinghouse on ongoing work.
UCLA’s current Dataverse collection page credits this “through [Marvick’s] efforts” and states UCLA was one of 8 founding members. The full institutional membership at founding was larger than 8: Erik Austin, a longtime ICPSR staff member, compiled a list of 22 original institutions from membership records, Michigan plus 21 others. Miller’s own August 1962 memo goes further: it names the members directly, dated “as of July 30, 1962,” and lists 21, “University of California at Los Angeles” among them. Either way, UCLA’s founding-member status is confirmed against the actual 1962 document, not just a later recollection.
That looked like the end of the “8” question, and then it got more interesting. ICPSR’s current director, Maggie Levenstein, used the same “8” figure independently during a UCLA visit, not obviously copying UCLA’s own page. And ICPSR’s own institutional archive at the Bentley Historical Library, per its finding aid, holds a folder titled “Committee of Eight, Correspondence and Minutes, 1962-1963.” That’s a plausible, specific referent for “8” that has nothing to do with the 21/22-institution membership count: a smaller founding committee, not the full roster of dues-paying members. If that’s right, both numbers could be correct, describing two different things. Not confirmed. Nobody has read that folder yet.






WarningThe headcount is fixed. The personal-role claim is now plausible, still not proven.



UCLA’s founding-member status is confirmed against the primary 1962 document itself. The personal-role question moved, but didn’t resolve. No source found so far, including Miller’s own founding memo, gives documentary evidence Marvick had a formal role in founding ICPSR in 1962. ICPSR’s first annual report names its initial council members, and he isn’t on it. But a 1999 memorial by Heinz Eulau, a colleague of both men, establishes something new: Marvick and Warren Miller were personal friends and research collaborators a full decade before either the archive or ICPSR existed, together at Michigan’s Survey Research Center in the early 1950s. That’s a real, documented channel through which “through his efforts” could plausibly be true, even though nobody has yet found a document that says so directly. His formally documented ICPSR role remains governing-board service starting 1964, rising to chair of the ICPR Council in 1966-67 (per Eulau, more precise than earlier sources), all after founding, not during it. “Marvick helped connect UCLA to the emerging ICPSR network, likely through his friendship with Miller” is now a defensible sentence. “Through his efforts, UCLA was one of the founding members” still isn’t, on direct documentary evidence. See Sources & Open Questions for the full research trail.



Marvick’s own scholarly profile
Apart from the ICPSR question, Marvick’s documented research program explains why an archive like this would plausibly come from him specifically: survey methods brought from Michigan in 1954, statistical approaches to political behavior, and, per a UC memorial, work as “an early advocate and practitioner of computer applications to political data.” His papers include election surveys, computer codebooks, and printouts spanning Los Angeles politics, the Detroit Area Study, West German elections, and Indian electorate surveys.
Eulau’s 1999 memorial fills in the earlier chapter of that career. Marvick arrived at Michigan’s Survey Research Center in the early 1950s, fresh off a Columbia PhD, as a Carnegie Fellow, working alongside Morris Janowitz on a restudy of the Center’s 1952 election data. Warren Miller was there too, still finishing his own PhD. The two became close, personally and professionally, years before either left Michigan, Miller for a stint at Berkeley, Marvick for UCLA, where Eulau writes he “took deep Western roots.” By 1956 Marvick was already organizing national conversations in the field: he named the three panels for the first APSA meeting sessions devoted exclusively to political behavior. He chaired APSA’s own 1972 annual meeting program at Eulau’s request, and in 1988 spent two days interviewing Eulau for the APSA oral history project, eight double-sided tapes, at his home in Los Angeles.






NoteWhat’s still not documented: why 1961, specifically



No source found so far, including Eulau’s detailed personal memoir, states Marvick’s own reason for founding the archive in 1961. That absence is notable on its own: Eulau’s memoir covers Marvick’s career in real depth, APSA leadership roles, ICPR council chairmanship, his broad intellectual range, his family, and never once mentions the archive. The scholarly profile above makes founding an archive a plausible, well-contextualized move for him, but his personal motivation remains an inference, not a documented fact. His own papers (correspondence, project records from roughly 1959 to 1964) are still the likeliest place that would actually resolve this. Marvick died of a stroke in late February 1999, four weeks after Miller; any direct account would have to come from those papers or from people who knew him, not from him.

title: Origins (1961–1977)
section: Merger into the Survey Research Center, 1964 (disputed)
text:
Merger into the Survey Research Center, 1964 (disputed)
Three internal sources (two 2017 slide decks and the Dataverse About page) agree that the archive merged into UCLA’s Survey Research Center (SRC) in 1964, “under Eve Fielder.” One deck adds detail: the PBA “merged with a planned Archive Data Library the SRC was to house.”






WarningOpen conflict: was Fielder SRC’s director from 1964?



A published obituary for Eve Fielder states she became SRC’s first director in 1976, the same year external evidence (UCLA’s General Catalog) places SRC’s incorporation into ISSR. This directly conflicts with the “1964, under Fielder” framing repeated across three internal sources. Two readings are possible: SRC existed from 1964 under a different, unidentified founding director and Fielder took over later, or the “1964 + Fielder” framing in the internal decks compresses two separate events into one. Not resolved. See Sources & Open Questions.

title: Origins (1961–1977)
text:
Toward 1977
What’s well-established: by the mid-1970s the archive was operating inside SRC, and by 1976–77 it was reconstituted as a service unit of the Institute for Social Science Research (ISSR). Exactly how SRC’s 1976 incorporation into ISSR relates to the archive’s own December 1977 establishment as a named ISSR unit is covered in the next chapter, The ISSR Era.

title: The ISSR Era (1977–2014)
text:
NoteAbout this chapter



Most of this chapter draws on a single deep-research pass (evidence/deep-research-report.md) that is heavily cited but not yet independently verified claim-by-claim. Treat names, dates, and titles here as well-sourced leads rather than settled fact until spot-checked against the primary documents it cites.
The archive’s 37 years under this institutional umbrella break into three distinct subperiods, not one continuous arrangement.

title: The ISSR Era (1977–2014)
text:
ISSR proper (1977 – late 2000s)
An international directory published through the OECD describes the ISSR Data Archive at UCLA as established in December 1977 to support quantitative research, “primarily secondary analysis.” Data came mainly through UCLA’s ICPSR membership, supplemented by federal statistical agencies (Census Bureau, National Center for Health Statistics, National Center for Education Statistics, Bureau of Labor Statistics) and locally produced studies such as the Los Angeles County Social Survey.

title: The ISSR Era (1977–2014)
text:
Renamed: Institute for Social Research (~2009–2011)
By the 2009–10 UCLA General Catalog, the parent institute’s name had changed to the Institute for Social Research (ISR): same phone number, new website (isr.ucla.edu), same components, including the Social Science Data Archive. No director has been identified for the institute under this name. The renamed institute still appears in the 2010–11 catalog.

title: The ISSR Era (1977–2014)
text:
Standalone SSDA (~2011–2014)
By the 2011–12 catalog, neither ISSR nor ISR appears as a named institute. The Social Science Data Archive is listed independently, as a Social Sciences collection, using its own website (dataarchives.ss.ucla.edu). No public source identifies a formal dissolution date or a single institutional successor for the parent institute.
Elizabeth “Libbie” Stephenson, the archive’s head archivist and later director, is the strongest through-line across this entire chapter. She started around 1977, the same year the archive became a named ISSR unit, and stayed through the 2014 Library transfer, retiring in 2016. That means one person’s tenure spans essentially the whole ISSR era end to end, plus two more years. By the early 2010s the archive was moving toward modern research-data curation practice: a 2013 conference paper documents SSDA experimenting with the DDI-Lifecycle metadata standard and Colectica curation software immediately before the Library transfer. See People for her full career profile and evidence/stephenson-icpsr-sources.md for sourcing.

NoteLibbie Stephenson: the single best-documented witness to this whole era



Her UCLA tenure runs almost exactly the length of the ISSR era itself: started around 1977, the same year the archive was formally reconstituted as a named ISSR unit, and continued through the 2014 Library transfer and two more years, retiring in 2016. BA Fine Arts (UC Riverside, 1975), MLS (UCLA, 1977). IASSIST President 1995–97. ICPSR Council 1996–2000. Won the 2007 William H. Flanigan Award for Distinguished Service as an ICPSR Official Representative, and a 2016 IASSIST achievement award shortly before retiring. See evidence/stephenson-icpsr-sources.md. Correction: an earlier note on this site said 2014; that was wrong. Two independent primary sources (the retirement article’s own date stamp, and its reference to the 2016 IASSIST conference in Bergen, Norway, confirmed independently) put it at 2016. She’s very likely the strongest oral-history candidate on this entire page: unlike Marvick or the ISSR-era directors, she retired only a decade ago.

Most pre-2014 names beyond Stephenson and Jamison come from a single deep-research pass and have not been independently verified against primary documents. See Sources & Open Questions.
The distinction between “ISSR/SRC staff generally” and “SSDA-specific staff” is often unclear in the sourcing. Several names above may have served the parent institute broadly rather than the archive specifically.
